docs.title: Kulp Lights Controller Manual
docs.text: This manual covers the hardware of the Kulp Lights controllers.

docs.title: PocketBeagle 2 controllers
docs.text:
• K8-Pro · K8-Max

    8 local pixel ports + 4 differential ports (16 strings).

    K8-Pro · K8-Max

  • K8-PB · K4-PB · K40D-PB

    Compact: 8 or 4 local pixel ports, or 40 strings on 10 differential ports (K40D-PB).

    K8-PB · K4-PB · K40D-PB

  • K16 · K16-Pro · K16-Max

    16 local pixel ports + 4 or 8 differential ports.

    K16 · K16-Pro · K16-Max

  • K32 · K32-Pro · K32-Max

    32 local pixel ports + 4 or 8 differential ports.

    K32 · K32-Pro · K32-Max

  • PocketScroller v2 · v3 · -16

    6, 8 or 16 HUB75 outputs for LED panel matrices.

    PocketScroller v2 · v3 · PocketScroller-16

docs.text:

    8 fused pixel ports + differential ports; the K8-B-Scroller adds 3 HUB75 panel outputs.

    K8-B · K8-B-Scroller

  • K64D-B · K128D-B

    64 or 128 strings on 16 or 32 differential ports, with audio and two DMX/LOR outputs.

    K64D-B · K128D-B

    OctoPlus

docs.title: Raspberry Pi controllers
docs.text:
• K8-Pi

    8 eFused pixel ports + 3 differential ports and an expansion port: 36 strings.

    K8-Pi

  • K2-Pi-Servo · K2-Pi0

    2 eFused pixel ports, plus 16 servo outputs (K2-Pi-Servo) or on a Pi Zero (K2-Pi0).

docs.title: Displays & add-ons
docs.text:
• BBB-OLED · Pi-OLED

    A status display, buttons and a clock for a BeagleBone or Pi running FPP. The PiOLED 3.0 adds high-quality audio.

    BBB-OLED · Pi-OLED

Every one of these boards is a cape (or hat) for a PocketBeagle 2, a BeagleBone Black or a Raspberry Pi and runs FPP (Falcon Player). FPP is the software that plays your show, and it has its own manual at manual.falconplayer.com. This manual doesn't repeat that one. It covers what the FPP manual can't:

  • Power: wiring power supplies, banks, fuses and eFuses.
  • Pixel outputs and differential ports: wiring pixels and receivers.
  • Controls & display: the buttons, the OLED menus and the status LEDs.
  • Board pages: one per controller, with specifications, connector maps and dimensions.
  • Troubleshooting for hardware problems.

Read the Safety page before you connect a power supply.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text: Start with the symptom closest to yours. For software problems (playlists, schedules, sequences), FPP's troubleshooting guide goes further.

docs.title: Nothing happens at power-up
docs.text: Check Why Is the logic power terminal powered? Only one terminal runs the controller: V1 on K16/K32, the right-hand terminal on K8. The other boards have one terminal. See Power. Is the blue LED beside that terminal lit? If not, there's no voltage at the terminal. Check the supply, the wiring and the polarity. Is the polarity right? Reversed power is blocked, not damaging, but the board stays off. Swap the wires. Is the second blue LED (5 V) lit? If the terminal LED is on but this one is off, contact support. PocketScroller (v3 or -16): is the supply 5 V? A higher voltage trips its input fuse. Disconnect it, wait a minute, and reconnect with 5 V.

docs.title: Power LEDs on, but the OLED stays blank
docs.text:
• Give it two minutes. The first boot of a new SD card takes longer.
  • Re-seat the SD card, and try another card or a freshly written image. A worn-out SD card is the most common cause.
  • Check the PocketBeagle 2 is seated fully and the right way round (PocketBeagle 2), or that the BeagleBone is fully on its headers (BeagleBone Black).
  • BeagleBone Black boards: an older BeagleBone (before about 2019) boots its own eMMC instead of the SD card. Hold its Boot button while you power up; see Booting from the SD card.
  • Raspberry Pi boards: check the hat is on all 40 header pins, not shifted by a row or column (Raspberry Pi).
  • BeagleBone Black boards: if FPP was shut down, the BeagleBone stays off until you press the cape's Power button or switch the supply off and on.
  • If FPP is reachable on the network but the OLED is dark, check Settings → System → Status Display.

docs.title: Can't find the controller on the network
docs.text:
• Read the IP address from the OLED status page. Make sure your computer is on the same network.
  • Check the Ethernet jack's LEDs. No link light means a cable or switch problem.
  • Make sure the cable is in the Ethernet jack (the one with LEDs), not a differential or DMX port.
  • No Ethernet? Plug in a USB Wi-Fi adapter and use the hotspot.
  • FPP's network troubleshooting covers subnets, static IPs and multiple interfaces.

docs.title: FPP doesn't recognise the board
docs.text:
If Pixel Strings shows no board, or Cape Info is empty:

  • Update FPP to the latest release. Older FPP versions don't know the newest boards.
  • Re-seat the PocketBeagle 2 or BeagleBone. The board ID is read over the header pins.
  • Make sure the PocketBeagle 2 boards have a PocketBeagle 2, not a PocketBeagle 1, and the BeagleBone boards a compatible BeagleBone.

docs.title: No pixels light
docs.text:
Work from the controller outwards:

  1. Port LED. Is the green LED next to the port lit?
    • Off, and the rest of the bank too: the bank has no power, or is switched off (Pro/Max) because nothing is playing. Run a test (step 2) and check again.
    • Off, just this port: blown fuse, or tripped/disabled eFuse (Max). See Port Status.
  2. Test pattern. Press Test on the controller. If the string lights, the hardware is fine and the problem is in the configuration: pixel count, start channel, or the sequence.
  3. Wiring. Check G D V order against the pigtail, and that the data wire goes to the string's input end (look for the arrows on the pixels).
  4. Voltage. Is the bank voltage right for the pixels? 12 V pixels on a 5 V bank stay dark or flicker.
  5. Protocol and count. In Pixel Strings, check the protocol (WS2811 for most pixels) and that the pixel count is more than 0.

docs.title: Only part of a string lights, or colours are wrong
docs.text:
• Colours wrong: set the correct colour order (RGB, GRB, …) for that port.
  • Stops partway: usually a failed pixel. The first dark pixel, or the last working one before it, is usually the bad one. On Max boards, Count Pixels on Port Status helps find it.
  • Ends dim or turn orange/pink: voltage drop. Inject power at the far end, from the same supply (see the power injection warning).

docs.title: Flicker or random colours
docs.text:
• Check that all supplies share a common ground with the controller.
  • Make sure only one source is sending data. Turn off any E1.31/DDP output in xLights while FPP is playing.
  • Long first run of bare data wire: add a null pixel, or move the string to a differential receiver.
  • Turn the brightness down to check whether it's a power problem.

docs.title: A fuse keeps blowing / an eFuse keeps tripping
docs.text: There is a real fault on that port. Unplug the string and see whether the port stays up. Then check the pigtail, the connectors and the string for shorts or water. On Max boards, look at the current on Port Status just before the trip. A string drawing close to 6 A on its own is simply too long for one port: split it or inject power.

docs.title: A differential receiver is dark
docs.text:
• Is the receiver powered? The RJ45 carries no power.
  • Press the receiver's test button. If it lights, the problem is the cable or the configuration.
  • Swap to a known-good Cat5e/Cat6 cable. A bad crimp on one pair kills one string.
  • In Pixel Strings, check the pixel counts for that port's four strings, and the receiver chain settings for smart receivers.

docs.title: Getting help
docs.text:
If you're stuck, email support@kulplights.com with:

  • the board model and revision (printed on the board)
  • the FPP version (Help → About)
  • a description of the problem and what you've already tried
  • photos of the wiring, if it's a wiring question
  • an FPP diagnostic report: Help → Troubleshooting, or press F8 in the FPP web UI (how)

The FPP forums and Facebook groups are also a good place to ask about software.

docs.title: Which model line?
docs.text:
• Base (K16, K32): the most outputs for the money. Fused ports and send-only differential.
  • Pro: adds two-way differential for Falcon V5 receivers, audio, a second DMX output, three USB ports, a fan header and expansion I/O. Bank power switching (K8-Pro, and K16-Pro/K32-Pro from v4.1).
  • Max: everything in Pro, plus an eFuse on every port. FPP can switch each port and read its current, and a short is cut in microseconds and reported in FPP instead of blowing a fuse.

docs.title: Displays & add-ons
docs.text: The BBB-OLED and Pi-OLED add a status display, menu buttons, a real-time clock and a temperature sensor to a BeagleBone Black or Raspberry Pi running FPP, with no outputs of their own. The PiOLED 3.0 also adds a high-quality line-level audio output.

docs.title: All boards
docs.text: All of them run FPP. The boards in the PocketBeagle 2 section need a PocketBeagle 2; the K4-PB, K40D-PB and PocketScroller v2 also work with the original PocketBeagle 1. See PocketBeagle 2, BeagleBone Black and Raspberry Pi.

docs.title: BBB-OLED
docs.text:
A small add-on for a plain BeagleBone Black running FPP: an OLED status display, four menu buttons, a real-time clock and a temperature sensor. It has no outputs of its own.

BBB-OLED (v2.0), shown without its display, which covers the clock battery.

This page describes revision v2.0 (printed on the board as BBB-OLED v2.0).

Use it on a BeagleBone that drives its lights over the network or USB, or plays the show as a player or master: it gives the BeagleBone the same display, menus and test buttons as the Kulp controllers. It plugs onto the BeagleBone's P9 header only.

Not with an output cape

The BBB-OLED uses pins on the P9 header that the BeagleBone Black output capes also use. Fit it to a BeagleBone without another cape.

docs.title: Specifications
docs.text: BBB-OLED Display 128×64 OLED, blue/yellow, fitted Buttons Up / Down / Back / Enter Real-time clock yes, CR1220 cell included Temperature sensor yes Headers 1×4 I²C socket; 2×5 I²C and GPIO header Outputs none Power from the BeagleBone Size 66.6 × 34.0 mm (2.62 × 1.34 in), no mounting holes Requires BeagleBone Black or compatible (see BeagleBone Black), FPP 9.5 or later

docs.title: Fitting it
docs.text:
1. Disconnect power from the BeagleBone.
  2. Line the BBB-OLED's socket up with the P9 header: the end marked P9 goes at the BeagleBone's Ethernet end, with the board lying over the BeagleBone.
  3. Press it down evenly until it is fully seated. It has no mounting holes; the header holds it.

The BBB-OLED takes its power from the BeagleBone. Power the BeagleBone from its barrel jack or USB as usual.

docs.title: Buttons
docs.text: The four buttons are in a diamond at the right: UP at the top, BACK at the left, ENTER at the right and DOWN at the bottom. DOWN also works as Test on the status page. See Controls & display.

docs.title: Clock
docs.text: The real-time clock keeps time with no network. Its CR1220 cell sits under the display: unplug the display to change it. See Clock.

docs.title: Headers
docs.text:
Header Marking Details I²C socket J3: GND 3.3V SCL SDA 1×4 socket at the top left, on the I²C bus, for an extra I²C sensor or device. GPIO / I²C J4: 3.3V SDA SCL 14 GND, 3.3V GND GPIO3 15 16 2×5 header below it, laid out like the first ten pins of a Raspberry Pi header: 3.3 V, GND, the I²C bus and three BeagleBone GPIOs (GPIO3_14, GPIO3_15 and GPIO3_16, on P9-31, P9-29 and P9-30). Unlike a Pi, it has 3.3 V only, no 5 V: some Pi I²C add-ons work if they run on 3.3 V.

The GPIO pins are 3.3 V only: use them for buttons or switches to ground in FPP's GPIO Inputs.

docs.title: FPP setup
docs.text: When FPP detects the BBB-OLED it sets up the display, the buttons, the clock and the temperature sensor automatically.

docs.title: K128D-B
docs.text:
One hundred and twenty-eight pixel strings from thirty-two differential ports, for driving differential receivers, plus two DMX/LOR outputs, built-in audio and an FM transmitter socket. It has no local pixel ports.

An early K128D-B (v1.0) with a BeagleBone fitted upside down. The current v1.1 has RJ45 jacks for the DMX outputs; the board map below shows it.

This page describes revision v1.1 (printed on the board as K128D-B v1.1). See Board revisions for v1.0.

How the K128D-B differs from the other boards

  • It needs a BeagleBone Black (or a compatible BeagleBone), which plugs in upside down on top of the cape. See BeagleBone Black.
  • Differential ports only. Every string goes out over an RJ45 to a differential receiver, which powers the pixels. There are no pixel plugs on the board.
  • 5 V only. The board takes a regulated 5 V supply for the controller alone.
  • About 80,000 pixels in all. The BeagleBone's processor, not the ports, sets the limit.
  • The differential ports are send-only: smart receivers work in v1, v2 or V4 mode. Falcon V5 receivers work in V4 mode, without status reports.

docs.text: K128D-B Local pixel ports none Differential ports 32 × RJ45 = 128 strings (1–128), send-only Pixel capacity up to 800 per string at 40 fps; about 80,000 in total Power input 5 V DC only, 2-pin 5.08 mm screw terminal (controller only) DMX / serial 2, RS-485 transmit, on RJ45 jacks with a DMX/LOR switch (ttyS1, ttyS2) Audio built-in stereo DAC, 3.5 mm line out, FM transmitter socket GPIO header 2×8: 3.3 V, 5 V, GND, I²C and 8 BeagleBone pins Ethernet & USB the BeagleBone's own Display & buttons 128×64 OLED, Up / Down / Back / Enter / Test, Boot, Power Real-time clock yes, CR1220 backup cell Temperature sensors 2 (Temp1, Temp2) Size 182.0 × 225.0 mm (7.17 × 8.86 in), 7 mounting holes, 3.2 mm FPP output BBShiftString Requires BeagleBone Black or compatible, FPP 9.5 or later

docs.title: Board map
docs.text: The BeagleBone mounts upside down over the two long headers at the top right, with its Ethernet jack over the notch in the right-hand edge.

docs.title: Power
docs.text:
The power terminal is on the right-hand edge, below the BeagleBone, marked 5V (upper screw) and GND (lower screw). It powers the BeagleBone and all of the logic, including the thirty-two differential driver chips. The receivers power the pixels from their own supplies. Use a regulated 5 V supply rated at least 4 A. The LED beside the terminal lights when the board has power. FPP shows no input voltage reading on this board.

5 V only

Use a regulated 5 V supply, and check that 5 V goes to the upper screw before you switch on. Don't connect 12 V or 24 V.

docs.title: Differential ports
docs.text:
The thirty-two jacks fill the lower part of the board in 8 rows of 4. They are vertical jacks: the cables plug in from above. Each carries four strings, numbered as printed beside it, across each row and then down:

Row 1 (top) 1-4 5-8 9-12 13-16 Row 2 17-20 21-24 25-28 29-32 Row 3 33-36 37-40 41-44 45-48 Row 4 49-52 53-56 57-60 61-64 Row 5 65-68 69-72 73-76 77-80 Row 6 81-84 85-88 89-92 93-96 Row 7 97-100 101-104 105-108 109-112 Row 8 (bottom) 113-116 117-120 121-124 125-128

The ports are send-only, with the standard four-strings-per-RJ45 pinout. Any standard differential receiver works, and smart receivers work in v1, v2 or V4 mode; with v2 you can chain up to six receivers on a port. Falcon V5 receivers also work, set to V4, but they can't send status back. See Differential ports.

docs.title: Pixel capacity
docs.text:
Each string can drive up to 800 pixels at 40 fps, or 1600 at 20 fps. All the strings are sent together, so the longest string sets the frame rate for the whole board.

The whole board tops out at about 80,000 pixels, because the BeagleBone's single processor prepares every pixel for every frame. Spread them across the ports however you like. Using the built-in audio takes some of that processor time, so the limit is a little lower when FPP plays audio from the board.

docs.title: DMX / LOR
docs.text:
The two serial outputs are RJ45 jacks at the top-left corner: ttyS1 on the left and ttyS2 on the right. Each has a small slide switch beside it:

Switch RJ45 pins Use DMX (up) Data + on pin 1, Data − on pin 2, ground on 7 and 8 DMX over RJ45, Renard, Pixelnet LOR (down) Data + on pin 4, Data − on pin 5, ground on 7 and 8 Light-O-Rama networks: plug straight into LOR controllers

The outputs are transmit-only. FPP calls them ttyS1 and ttyS2. See DMX / serial.

docs.title: Audio and FM transmitter
docs.text: The board has a built-in PCM5102A stereo DAC. Its 3.5 mm line-out jack is in the notch on the top edge, and the FM transmitter socket (RST … L R) is beside it, for an optional Si4713 module. See Audio.

docs.title: GPIO header
docs.text:
The 2×8 header beside the Test button brings out power, the I²C bus and eight BeagleBone pins, for extra buttons, switches or I²C sensors:

Pin Signal Pin Signal 1 3.3 V 2 5 V 3 SDA 4 5 V 5 SCL 6 GND 7 P8-27 8 P8-17 9 GND 10 P8-16 11 P8-18 12 P8-13 13 P8-15 14 GND 15 P8-14 16 P8-19

Pin 1 is at the bottom left; the signal names are printed above and below the pins. Use the pins in FPP's GPIO Inputs, under their BeagleBone names. They connect straight to the BeagleBone, so they are 3.3 V only: wire buttons to switch a pin to GND and use the pull-up mode.

docs.title: Buttons
docs.text: Button Details Up Down Back Enter the menu buttons, at the left below the OLED. Controls & display Test to the right of the menu buttons. Test button Boot below the BeagleBone. Hold it at power-on to boot an older BeagleBone from its SD card; see Booting from the SD card. Pressing it while the board is running briefly glitches strings 65–72. Power left of the power terminal. Shuts down or restarts the BeagleBone; see Power button.

docs.title: FPP setup
docs.text: When FPP detects the K128D-B it sets itself up automatically. It enables the K128D-B pixel-string layout (FPP's BBShiftString output, with all 128 strings at 100 pixels each), the built-in audio, the temperature sensors, the FM transmitter plugin's settings, and two disabled DMX outputs on ttyS1 and ttyS2. Set the pixel counts and start channels from xLights or the FPP Pixel Strings page. See Configuring outputs.

docs.title: Board revisions
docs.text: Revision Changes v1.0 The two DMX outputs are 3-pin pluggable terminals (G - +), with no DMX/LOR switch, and the differential jacks are surface-mount parts. v1.1 DMX outputs on RJ45 jacks with DMX/LOR switches, sturdier through-hole differential jacks, and an electronic fuse on the power input.

docs.title: Dimensions & mounting
docs.text:
• 182.0 × 225.0 mm (7.17 × 8.86 in), 7 plated mounting holes, 3.2 mm, for M3 (or #4) screws and standoffs.
  • Use standoffs at least 6 mm (¼ in) tall, so nothing on the underside touches the enclosure.

docs.text:
16 eFused pixel ports with per-port current monitoring, 8 two-way differential ports, audio and 2 DMX.

K16-Max with a PocketBeagle 2 fitted. Photos may show an earlier board revision.

This page describes revision v4.1.0 (printed on the board as K16-Max v4.1.0). Differences in earlier revisions are listed under Board revisions.

docs.title: K16A-B
docs.text:
The K16A-B was a BeagleBone Black pixel controller: 16 pixel ports, 4 differential ports and an expansion port, for 48 strings in all, plus audio and two DMX outputs.

K16A-B v3.0, powered, with a BeagleBone Black fitted.

Retired

The K16A-B is no longer sold. This page is for the many boards still in use. Its successors are the PocketBeagle 2 K16, K16-Pro and K16-Max.

The K16A-B went through three generations. They share the layout, connectors and FPP setup, but differ in power and port protection, so check which one you have. The revision is printed on the board, under the name (K16A-B v3.0.1).

Generation Revisions Made Power terminals Port protection v1 v1.0.0 – v1.2 2020–2022 2 5 A mini-blade fuses v2 v2.0, v2.1 2023–2024 2 eFuses, about 5.2 A v3 v3.0, v3.0.1 2024–2025 4 eFuses, about 6 A

How the K16A-B differs from the PocketBeagle 2 boards

  • It needs a BeagleBone Black (or a compatible BeagleBone). See BeagleBone Black.
  • The power terminals don't all have the same polarity. Check the markings on each one.
  • Only one terminal runs the controller: the right-hand one.

docs.text:

All three need a BeagleBone Black or compatible and run on FPP 9.5 or later.

docs.title: Board map
docs.text:
v3.0.1. The v1 and v2 boards have the same layout above the pixel ports; below them they have two power terminals with the fuses (v1) between them.

The BeagleBone sits underneath the board, with its Ethernet jack in the notch in the right-hand edge.

docs.title: Power
docs.text:
v3v2v1

Four terminals along the bottom edge, one per bank of four ports. The polarity alternates from one terminal to the next:

Terminal Marking Left screw Right screw Powers 1st (left) V+ 1-4 G V+ ports 1–4 2nd V+ 5-8 V+ G ports 5–8 3rd V+ 9-12 G V+ ports 9–12 4th (right) V+ 13-16 V+ G ports 13–16, and the BeagleBone and all the logic
  • The board won't start without power on the right-hand V+ 13-16 terminal, even with the others powered.
  • Each bank can run its own voltage, 5–24 V, so 5, 12 and 24 V pixels can share the board on different banks.
  • FPP shows the four voltages as VIN1–VIN4. Two blue LEDs on the right-hand edge show that the right-hand terminal has power and that the 5 V supply is running.
  • Only the controller's own supply (the right-hand terminal) is protected against a reversed supply. A reversed supply on any terminal can damage that bank's ports.

Two terminals along the bottom edge:

Terminal Left screw Right screw Powers left G V+ ports 1–8 right V+ G ports 9–16, and the BeagleBone and all the logic
  • The board won't start without power on the right-hand terminal.
  • Each terminal can run its own voltage, 5–18 V. Don't use 24 V supplies.
  • FPP shows the two voltages as VIN1 and VIN2.
  • The controller's own supply is protected against a reversed supply; the pixel ports aren't.

Two terminals along the bottom edge, with the fuses between them:

Terminal Left screw Right screw Powers left G V+ ports 1–8 right V+ G ports 9–16, and the BeagleBone and all the logic
  • 5 V or 12 V only, 12 V maximum. Don't use 24 V supplies.
  • The 3-pin Input Voltage Select jumper must match the supply on the right-hand terminal: 5V for a 5 V supply, 12V for 12 V.
  • The board won't start without power on the right-hand terminal.
  • FPP shows the two voltages as VIN1 and VIN2.
  • The pixel ports aren't protected against a reversed supply. Check the polarity of each terminal before you power up.

See Power for supply sizing and safety.

docs.title: Powering the BeagleBone: the "power BBB" jumper
docs.text: The jumper marked Jumper to power BBB from board, on the right-hand side, connects the board's 5 V supply to the BeagleBone. It is fitted at the factory; leave it fitted. With it removed, the BeagleBone needs its own supply in its barrel jack. Never fit the jumper and plug a supply into the BeagleBone's barrel jack at the same time.

docs.title: Pixel ports
docs.text:
The sixteen pixel ports are in two rows across the lower part of the board:

Top row PT1 PT3 PT5 PT7 PT9 PT11 PT13 PT15 Bottom row PT2 PT4 PT6 PT8 PT10 PT12 PT14 PT16

Each port is G D V (ground, data, +V), as printed beneath it. PT1 is FPP port 1, and so on. On v1 boards the bottom row is offset half a step to the right. Each port can drive up to 800 pixels at 40 fps. See Pixel outputs.

v2 and v3: eFusesv1: fuses

Every port has its own eFuse, which trips at about 6 A (v3) or 5.2 A (v2) and latches off. FPP reads every port's current and switches each port on and off as needed. When an eFuse trips, FPP marks the port with a red icon on Status/Control → Port Status; click it to turn the port back on once the fault is fixed. The LED by each port lights when the port has power. See Current monitoring.

Each port has its own 5 A mini-blade fuse, in a row along the bottom edge. The LED by each fuse lights when the fuse is good and the bank has power. See Power → Fuses.

docs.title: Differential ports
docs.text:
The four jacks are in a 2 × 2 block in the upper middle of the board, numbered across the top row and then the bottom row:

left right Top 17-20 21-24 Bottom 25-28 29-32

Each jack carries four strings, with the standard pinout. See Differential ports.

  • v1: send-only. Smart receivers work in v1, v2 or V4 mode; Falcon V5 receivers work set to V4, without status reports.
  • v2 and v3: the first pair of each jack is two-way, so Falcon V5 receivers can report back. On v2, that needs a cape EEPROM from April 2024 or later: update it under Help → About → Cape Info (see Updating). v3 boards have it already.

docs.title: Expansion port (strings 33–48)
docs.text:
v2 and v3v1

The 24-pin, 2×12 shrouded header on the top edge carries 16 more pixel strings, for a Falcon F16v4-style expansion board, which turns them into pixel ports with their own power. The pinout is the same as the K8-PB's: GND on pins 1, 2 and 22, +5 V on 3 and 4, and strings 33–48 on pins 5–20 in order (string 33 on pin 5, 34 on pin 6, and so on). Pin 1 is at the right-hand end, on the outer (board-edge) row.

The lines are driven at 5 V by the board's shift registers, so they can't be used as GPIO inputs.

The 40-pin, 2×20 header on the top edge carries 16 more pixel strings, for a Falcon F16v3 expansion board. The pinout is the same as the K8-B's, with strings 33–48 in place of 21–36. The lines come straight from the BeagleBone at 3.3 V: always go through an expansion board.

docs.title: DMX
docs.text:
v2 and v3v1

Two RJ45 jacks on the left-hand edge: ttyS2 above ttyS1. Each is wired for DMX over RJ45:

RJ45 pin Signal DMX XLR pin 1 Data + 3 2 Data − 2 7, 8 Ground 1

There is no LOR setting: use an adapter for LOR, Renard or Pixelnet. See DMX / serial.

Two 3-pin pluggable terminals on the left-hand edge: ttyS1 above ttyS2 (the other way round from v2 and v3). From top to bottom each is Data +, Data −, Ground. Wire them to XLR pins 3, 2 and 1. See DMX / serial.

The outputs are transmit-only. FPP sets up a disabled DMX output on each.

docs.title: Audio and FM transmitter
docs.text: The built-in PCM5102A stereo DAC drives the 3.5 mm line-out jack at the top-left corner. The 11-pin FM transmitter socket along the top edge (R L GND 3.3V SDA SCL P9-22) takes the optional Si4713 FM transmitter. See Audio.

docs.title: K2-Pi-Servo
docs.text:
Two eFused pixel ports and 16 servo outputs on a Raspberry Pi hat, for props that move as well as light up.

K2-Pi-Servo (v1.0).

This page describes revision v1.0 (printed on the board as K2-Pi-Servo v1.0), the only revision.

How the K2-Pi-Servo differs from the other boards

  • It needs a Raspberry Pi 3 B+, 4 or 5. See Raspberry Pi.
  • Two power terminals: one (5–24 V) for the Pi and the two pixel ports, and a separate one for the servos. The two terminals have their screws in the opposite order.
  • No differential ports, DMX or real-time clock.

docs.title: Specifications
docs.text: K2-Pi-Servo Local pixel ports 2 (Port 1, Port 2), 3-pin 3.5 mm pluggable, plugs included Port protection eFuse per port, about 6 A, latching Power switching per port (FPP-controlled) Current monitoring both ports Pixels per string up to 1600; about 800 at 40 fps Servo outputs 16, standard 3-pin servo headers (signal, V+, GND) Power inputs pixels & Pi: 5–24 V DC. Servos: separate terminal, typically 5–6 V. DMX / serial none Audio the Pi's own Ethernet & USB the Pi's own Display & buttons 128×64 OLED, Up / Down / Back / Enter / Test Real-time clock none Temperature sensor yes Size 76.4 × 56.0 mm (3.01 × 2.20 in), 4 mounting holes, 2.7 mm FPP output DPIPixels (pixels), Servos (PCA9685) Requires Raspberry Pi 3 B+, 4 or 5, FPP 10 or later

docs.title: Board map
docs.text: The Pi sits under the board, with its USB and Ethernet ports sticking out past the right-hand edge. The terminals and pixel ports overhang the other end of the Pi.

docs.title: Power terminals
docs.text:
There are two power terminals on the left-hand edge:

Terminal Marking Screws, top to bottom Powers Pixel / Pi (top left) G, V+ 5-24V G, then V+ the Pi, the board's logic and both pixel ports Servo (bottom left) Servo V+, G V+, then G the 16 servos' V+ pins only

The two terminals are wired in opposite order

On the top terminal G is the upper screw; on the servo terminal V+ is the upper screw. Check each one against the markings before you power up.

Pixel / Pi terminal:

  • The pixels run at the supply voltage, so both strings must match it: 5, 12 or 24 V.
  • With a 5 V supply, turn its output up to about 5.3 V so the Pi gets a full 5 V; see Raspberry Pi → Powering.
  • The Pi and the logic are protected against a reversed supply, but the pixel ports aren't.
  • FPP shows its voltage as VIN Pixel.

Servo terminal:

  • Connect a supply that matches your servos, typically 5–6 V, sized for all the servos moving at once. The Pi and the pixels don't need it.
  • It goes straight to the servo headers, with no fuse and no reverse-polarity protection. A reversed supply reaches every servo.
  • FPP shows its voltage as VIN Servo.

docs.title: Pixel ports
docs.text:
The two pixel ports are on the left-hand edge between the terminals: Port 1 above Port 2. Each is G D V from top to bottom (ground, data, +V). Each string can have up to 1600 pixels; see Raspberry Pi → Pixel outputs.

Each port has its own eFuse, which trips at about 6 A and latches off, and FPP reads both ports' current. When an eFuse trips, FPP marks the port with a red icon on Status/Control → Port Status; click it to turn the port back on once the fault is fixed. The green LED beside each port lights when the port has power. See Current monitoring.

docs.title: Servo outputs
docs.text:
The 16 servo outputs are three rows of pins along the bottom edge, numbered 1 to 16 from left to right. Each column is one servo:

Row Marking Servo wire top (yellow) PWM signal (yellow, orange or white) middle (red) V+ power (red) bottom (black) GND ground (black or brown)

Plug each servo in with its signal wire towards the top of the board. The signal is 5 V.

Set the servos up in FPP under Input/Output Setup → Channel Outputs → Servos. For each output you set its start channel, its minimum and maximum pulse width (500–2500 µs; the default 1000–2000 µs suits most servos), and what it does when its channel is zero (hold, go to the minimum, maximum or centre, or stop). The frequency (50 Hz by default) applies to all 16. The Servo Position command moves a servo from a playlist, a button or a schedule. The outputs can also dim small LEDs instead of driving servos.

docs.text:
Connector Marking Details OLED GND VDD SCK SDA Controls & display Buttons Up Down Back Enter, Test the menu buttons in a cross at the right, with Test below them. Controls & display GPIO / I²C GND GND, 3.3V SDA SCL, 26 29 31 32 33 2×5 header, bottom right: ground, 3.3 V, the I²C bus (for an add-on clock or sensor) and five Pi GPIO pins, numbered by their Pi header pin. Use them in FPP's GPIO Inputs. 3.3 V only: wire buttons to switch a pin to GND.

The board has no real-time clock: set up NTP under Settings → Time, or add an I²C clock module on the GPIO / I²C header.

docs.text:
The smallest controller: two eFused pixel ports with current monitoring, on a hat the size of a Raspberry Pi Zero.

K2-Pi0 (v1.0).

This page describes revision v1.0 (printed on the board as K2-Pi0 v1.0), the only revision.

How the K2-Pi0 differs from the other boards

  • It's made for a Raspberry Pi Zero 2 W. See Raspberry Pi and Fitting it to a Pi.
  • No Ethernet: the Pi Zero 2 W has Wi-Fi only.
  • No display or buttons, no DMX and no real-time clock. Set it up and control it from FPP's web page.

docs.title: Power terminal
docs.text:
The power terminal is at the bottom left, marked G (left screw) and V+ 5-24V (right screw). It powers the Pi and both pixel ports. FPP shows its voltage as VIN.

  • The pixels run at the supply voltage, so both strings must match it: 5, 12 or 24 V.
  • With a 5 V supply, turn its output up to about 5.3 V so the Pi gets a full 5 V; see Raspberry Pi → Powering.
  • The Pi is protected against a reversed supply, but the pixel ports aren't. Check the polarity before you power up.
  • Don't plug a supply into the Pi's own USB power socket while the K2-Pi0 is powered.

docs.title: Pixel ports
docs.text:
The two pixel ports, PT1 (left) and PT2 (right), are in the middle of the board. Each is G D V (ground, data, +V), as printed beneath it. Each string can have up to 1600 pixels; see Raspberry Pi → Pixel outputs.

Each port has its own eFuse, which trips at about 6 A and latches off, and FPP reads both ports' current. When an eFuse trips, FPP marks the port with a red icon on Status/Control → Port Status; click it to turn the port back on once the fault is fixed. The green LED beside each port lights when the port has power. See Current monitoring.

docs.title: GPIO / I²C header
docs.text: The 2×5 header at the left-hand end brings out 3.3 V, ground, the I²C bus and five Pi GPIO pins, numbered on the board by their Pi header pin: 7, 8, 10, 11 and 13. Use them in FPP's GPIO Inputs for buttons or switches to ground, or add an I²C display or clock module. They are 3.3 V only.

docs.title: Fitting it to a Pi
docs.text:
On a Pi Zero 2 W (or Zero W), the K2-Pi0's four holes line up with the Pi's: fix them together with M2.5 standoffs.

It also works on the bigger Pis (3 B+, 4, 5), but there its holes don't line up with anything. The board is held only by the GPIO header, so make sure it can't tip or press down onto the Pi, where it could short something out. Support it with something insulating, and keep it clear of the Pi's components.

docs.title: FPP setup
docs.text:
When FPP detects the K2-Pi0 it sets itself up automatically. It enables the K2-Pi0 pixel-string layout (FPP's DPIPixels output, with 100 pixels on each port) and the voltage and current sensors. Set the pixel counts and start channels from xLights or the FPP Pixel Strings page. See Configuring outputs.

For the first setup, connect to FPP's Wi-Fi hotspot and join the Pi to your Wi-Fi network. Because the board has no clock, set up NTP under Settings → Time so schedules run at the right time.

docs.title: K32A-B
docs.text:
The K32A-B was a BeagleBone Black pixel controller: 32 fused pixel ports and 4 differential ports, for 48 strings in all, plus audio and two DMX outputs.

An early K32A-B (v1.0.0) with a BeagleBone Black fitted underneath. The current board differs in small details; the board map below shows it.

Retired

The K32A-B is no longer sold. This page is for the many boards still in use. Its successors are the PocketBeagle 2 K32, K32-Pro and K32-Max.

This page describes revision v1.3.1 (printed on the board as K32A-B v1.3.1), and notes where earlier boards differ. See Board revisions.

How the K32A-B differs from the PocketBeagle 2 boards

  • It needs a BeagleBone Black (or a compatible BeagleBone). See BeagleBone Black.
  • Four power terminals, one per bank of eight ports. Only the bottom-right one runs the controller.
  • Boards before v1.3 have an Input Voltage Select jumper and take 5 or 12 V only.
  • The differential ports are send-only: smart receivers work in v1, v2 or V4 mode.

docs.text: The BeagleBone sits underneath the middle of the board, with its Ethernet jack in the notch in the right-hand edge.

docs.title: Power
docs.text:
Four terminals, one in each corner. Each powers one bank of eight ports through their fuses. On every terminal G is the outer screw, nearer the corner, and V+ the inner one.

Terminal Marking Powers bottom left G V ports 1–8 bottom right V G ports 9–16, and the BeagleBone and all the logic top left G V ports 17–24 top right V G ports 25–32
  • The board won't start without power on the bottom-right terminal, even with the others powered.
  • Each bank can run its own voltage, so 5 and 12 V pixels can share the board on different banks.
  • v1.3 and later: 5–18 V on any terminal. Don't use 24 V supplies.
  • Before v1.3: 5 or 12 V only, 12 V maximum. The 3-pin Input Voltage Select jumper, at the lower right, must match the supply on the bottom-right terminal: 5V for 5 V, 12V for 12 V.
  • FPP shows the four voltages as VIN1 (ports 1–8), VIN2 (9–16), VIN3 (17–24) and VIN4 (25–32).
  • On v1.3.1 two blue LEDs on the right-hand side show that the bottom-right terminal has power and that the 5 V supply is running.
  • The terminals are rated 30 A. Use 10 or 12 AWG wire for heavily loaded banks.

Check polarity before you power up

The pixel ports aren't protected against a reversed supply: it goes straight through the fuses to that bank's ports and any pixels connected. From v1.3 the controller itself is protected.

See Power for supply sizing and safety.

docs.text: The jumper marked Jumper to power BBB from board, on the right-hand side above the BeagleBone's Ethernet jack, connects the board's 5 V supply to the BeagleBone. It is fitted at the factory; leave it fitted. With it removed, the BeagleBone needs its own supply in its barrel jack. Never fit the jumper and plug a supply into the BeagleBone's barrel jack at the same time.

docs.text:
The ports are in two blocks of sixteen, with the fuses along the outer edges. In each block the two rows are offset half a step:

Each port is G D V (ground, data, +V), as printed beneath it. PT1 is FPP port 1, and so on. Each port can drive up to 800 pixels at 40 fps. See Pixel outputs.

Each port has its own 5 A mini-blade fuse: F1–F16 along the bottom edge and F17–F32 along the top, left to right. The LED beside each fuse lights when the fuse is good and the bank has power. See Power → Fuses.

docs.text:

left right Top 33-36 37-40 Bottom 41-44 45-48

docs.title: K4-PB
docs.text:
The smallest pixel controller: 4 eFused pixel ports with per-port current monitoring and a DMX header, on a 71 × 67 mm board that fits a small TA-200 enclosure.

This page describes revision v3.0.1 (printed on the board as K4-PB v3.0.1). The K4-PB works with both the PocketBeagle 2 and the original PocketBeagle 1, and nothing blocks the SD card slot.

How the K4-PB differs from the K8, K16 and K32 boards

  • No Ethernet on the board. Plug a USB Ethernet adapter or an FPP-supported USB Wi-Fi adapter into its USB-A port. You need one of them to set it up. A "nano" or "mini" Wi-Fi adapter fits inside a TA-200 enclosure.
  • One power terminal, 5 or 12 V. It powers the controller and all four ports, so all of them run at the same voltage. 18 V is the absolute maximum; don't use 24 V supplies.
  • No differential ports and no expansion port. It drives only its four local ports.
  • DMX is a 3-pin header, not an RJ45 jack.
  • No real-time clock. The board gets the time from the network (NTP).
  • Not protected against a reversed supply. Check the polarity before you power up.

PocketBeagle 1: never connect its USB port to a computer

With an original PocketBeagle 1 fitted, don't power or set up the K4-PB through the PocketBeagle's own USB port (USB tethering). It can permanently damage the K4-PB. Power it only from its power terminal, and set it up over a USB network adapter. With a PocketBeagle 2, USB tethering is safe.

docs.title: Power terminal
docs.text:
The power terminal is at the bottom left: GND on the left screw, V+ on the right. It powers the PocketBeagle, the USB port and all of the logic, and all four pixel ports. FPP shows its voltage as VIN.

  • Every port shares this supply, so all four strings must be the same voltage: 5 V or 12 V pixels.
  • 18 V is the maximum. A 24 V supply will damage the board.
  • Two blue LEDs on the right-hand edge show that the board has power and that its internal 5 V supply is running.

Check polarity before you power up

The K4-PB is not protected against a reversed supply. The controller's own logic is protected, but a supply wired backwards drives the input surge-protection diode, which is likely to burn out. It usually fails as a short, and the board then won't power up until it is repaired.

docs.title: Pixel ports
docs.text: The four pixel ports are in a row across the middle of the board, PT1 on the left to PT4 on the right. Each is G D V (ground, data, +V), as printed beneath it. PT1 is FPP port 1, and so on. See Pixel outputs.

docs.title: eFuses and current monitoring
docs.text: Every port has its own eFuse, which trips at about 5.2 A and latches off. FPP reads every port's current and turns each port on and off as needed. When an eFuse trips, FPP marks the port with a red icon on Status/Control → Port Status; click it to turn the port back on once the fault is fixed. See Current monitoring.

docs.title: DMX
docs.text:
DMX is on the 3-pin, 2.54 mm header on the left edge, marked ttyS4:

Pin Marking Signal DMX XLR pin top G Ground 1 middle - Data − 2 bottom + Data + 3

Make up a cable from a 3-pin socket to an XLR or RJ45 DMX connector, wired as above. The output is transmit-only and can also drive Renard, LOR or Pixelnet through a suitable adapter. FPP calls the port ttyS4. See DMX / serial.

DMX on a PocketBeagle 2 with an older EEPROM

On a PocketBeagle 2, FPP finds this DMX port through a mapping in the cape EEPROM, added in EEPROM 3.0.1 (February 2025). On a board programmed before then, a DMX output on ttyS4 goes to the wrong serial port and nothing comes out. Fix it by updating the cape EEPROM under Help → About → Cape Info (see Updating), or set the DMX output's port to ttyS5 instead. On a PocketBeagle 1, ttyS4 always works.

docs.text: The 2×4 header position at the top right is not fitted: solder in a 2×4, 2.54 mm pin header if you want to use it. It brings out 3.3 V, GND and six PocketBeagle pins, numbered on the board: P1-2, P1-4, P1-6, P1-8, P1-10, P1-12. Use them in FPP's GPIO Inputs for buttons or switches to ground. When FPP detects the K4-PB it sets itself up automatically. For the first setup, plug in a USB Ethernet adapter and connect it to your network, or use a USB Wi-Fi adapter and FPP's Wi-Fi hotspot. Because the board has no clock, set up NTP under Settings → Time so schedules run at the right time.

docs.title: K40D-PB
docs.text:
Forty pixel strings from ten differential ports, for driving differential receivers. It has no local pixel ports.

K40D-PB (v3.0) shown with an original PocketBeagle (PocketBeagle 1) fitted.

This page describes revision v3.0 (printed on the board as K40D-PB v3.0). Designed for the original PocketBeagle, it works with both the PocketBeagle 2 and the PocketBeagle 1.

How the K40D-PB differs from the other boards

  • Differential ports only. Every string goes out over an RJ45 to a differential receiver, which powers the pixels. There are no pixel plugs on the board.
  • 5 V only. The board takes a regulated 5 V supply for the controller alone. Use one rated 4–5 A: the ten differential driver chips draw quite a bit.
  • No Ethernet on the board. Plug a USB Ethernet adapter or an FPP-supported USB Wi-Fi adapter into its USB-A port. You need one of them to set it up.
  • The USB-A port covers the PocketBeagle 2's SD card slot. Either use a PocketBeagle 2 Industrial, which runs FPP from its built-in eMMC, or fit the PB2 microSD extender, which clears the USB port.
  • DMX is a 3-pin pluggable terminal, not an RJ45 jack.

Never connect the PocketBeagle's USB port to a computer

Don't power or set up the K40D-PB through the PocketBeagle's own USB port (USB tethering). It can permanently damage the K40D-PB. Power it only from its 5 V terminal, and set it up over a USB network adapter.

docs.text:
Sixty-four pixel strings from sixteen differential ports, for driving differential receivers, plus two DMX/LOR outputs, built-in audio and an FM transmitter socket. It has no local pixel ports.

docs.text:
The sixteen jacks are in a 4 × 4 grid on the lower part of the board. Each carries four strings, numbered as printed beside it, across each row and then down:

docs.text:
Pixels and LED panels from one BeagleBone Black: 8 fused pixel ports, a differential port for 4 more strings, and 3 HUB75 outputs for LED panels.

K8-B-Scroller (v1.1.0), shown without a BeagleBone fitted.

This page describes revision v1.1.0 (printed on the board as K8-B-Scroller v1.1.0). See Board revisions for the earlier v1.0.

How the K8-B-Scroller differs from the other boards

  • Mini-blade fuses, not eFuses: no per-port switching or current readings.
  • Two DMX outputs on a 6-pin header, not RJ45 jacks.
  • The differential port is send-only: smart receivers work in v1, v2 or V4 mode. Falcon V5 receivers work in V4 mode, without status reports.

docs.text:
The jumper marked Jumper to Power BBB, to the right of the Test button, connects the board's 5 V regulator to the BeagleBone. It is fitted at the factory, and the BeagleBone then runs from the power terminal. Leave it fitted.

With the jumper removed, the BeagleBone isn't powered by the cape, and needs its own 5 V supply in its barrel jack. That isn't recommended. Never fit the jumper and plug a supply into the BeagleBone's barrel jack at the same time.

How the K8-PB differs from the other boards

  • The expansion port drives 16 more strings through a Falcon F16v4-style expansion board.
  • The differential ports are send-only. FPP drives this board with its BBB48String output, which doesn't support Falcon V5 smart receivers (V4 and earlier work).

docs.title: Power terminal
docs.text:
The K8-PB has one power terminal, at the bottom left, marked G (left screw) and V+ 5-18V (right screw). It powers the PocketBeagle 2, the USB port and all of the logic, and every pixel port. FPP shows its voltage as VIN.

  • Because every port shares this supply, all eight local strings must be the same voltage: 5 V or 12 V pixels. To mix voltages, put the other strings on differential receivers, which power their strings from their own supply.
  • 18 V is the maximum. A 24 V supply will damage the board.
  • The terminal is rated 32 A. With eight ports that can each draw up to about 5 A, add up your real loads and keep the total under that. Use 10 AWG wire for heavily loaded boards.
  • Two blue LEDs on the right-hand edge show power: the lower one lights when the terminal has power, and the upper one (beside the USB port) when the internal 5 V supply is running.

Check polarity before you power up

Unlike the K8, K16 and K32 boards, the K8-PB is not protected against a reversed supply. The controller's own logic is protected, but a supply wired backwards drives the input surge-protection diode, which is likely to burn out. It usually fails as a short, and the board then won't power up until it is repaired. Check that V+ goes to the right-hand screw and G to the left before you switch on.

See Power for supply sizing and safety.

docs.title: OctoPlus
docs.text:
Eight HUB75 outputs for LED panel matrices on a BeagleBone Black: an updated version of the classic "Octoscroller" cape, with a clock, a temperature sensor, an OLED and buttons.

An early OctoPlus (v2.2), without the OLED fitted. The board map below shows the current board.

This page describes revision v2.3.1 (printed on the board as OctoPlus v2.3.1). See Board revisions for the earlier boards.

How the OctoPlus differs from the other boards

  • It needs a BeagleBone Black (or a compatible BeagleBone). See BeagleBone Black.
  • 5 V only. The terminal powers the BeagleBone and the cape. The panels need their own 5 V supply.
  • No E line, so 1/32-scan panels (such as 64×64 1/32) don't work. 1/16-scan and lower do.
  • No mounting holes. The cape is held by its headers on the BeagleBone; mount the BeagleBone.

Use a USB sound card. docs.text:
The power terminal is on the tab at the top-right corner, marked 5V (left screw) and G (right screw).

  • It powers the BeagleBone and the cape. Use a regulated 5 V supply rated at least 2 A, more if you plug anything into the BeagleBone's USB port.
  • The panels are not powered through the OctoPlus. Run each panel's power from your 5 V panel supply. You can feed the OctoPlus from the same supply.
  • There are no power LEDs. When the board is running, the OLED shows status.

5 V only

The OctoPlus has no voltage regulator. A 12 V or 24 V supply, or a reversed one, makes the protection clamp conduct and trip the resettable fuse, and can damage the board.

docs.text:
The eight outputs are in two rows of four between the BeagleBone's headers. With the Ethernet jack at the top:

Top row Output 8 Output 7 Output 6 Output 5 Bottom row Output 4 Output 3 Output 2 Output 1

Each is a standard HUB75 connector, except that pin 8 is ground instead of E:

  • FPP allows up to 16 panels per output. The refresh rate depends on the longest chain and on the colour depth; see Capacity & refresh rate.

docs.title: Capacity & refresh rate
docs.text:
How many panels you can run depends on how long each chain is and on the colour depth. The table gives the full-frame refresh rate in Hz for 64×32 1/16-scan panels with all eight outputs in use, measured on an OctoPlus at FPP's default brightness (10). Bold values are 60 Hz or more. Italic values are under 60 Hz, where flicker starts to show on camera and to some viewers.

Panels per output Total panels 12-bit 10-bit 8-bit 6-bit 1 8 111 132 212 257 2 16 79 95 138 177 3 24 59.9 73 99 130 4 32 48 58 74 96 5 40 40 48 60 78 6 48 34 41 50 65 8 64 26 30 38 49 10 80 20 24 30 39 12 96 17 21 26 34 16 128 13 16 19 26
  • Rule of thumb at 60 Hz with 64×32 panels: 2–3 panels per output at 12-bit colour, or 5 per output at 8-bit (40 panels).
  • Smaller panels go further. A 32×16 P10 panel holds a quarter of the pixels of a 64×32, so a chain of P10s refreshes about as fast as a chain of a quarter as many 64×32s.
  • Refresh depends on the longest chain. Spread the panels evenly across the outputs.
  • A single chain on Output 1 runs up to twice as fast, because Output 1 shares its I/O bank with the panel control lines. Adding a second output costs most of that gain; going from 2 to 8 outputs costs only another 10–15 %.
  • These are worst-case figures, measured with random pixel data. Frames with flat or solid areas refresh faster: a solid fill ran 44 % faster at 3 panels per output, 8-bit.
  • 1/8-scan outdoor panels refresh about the same from 4 panels per output up, and faster on shorter chains (158 Hz at 1 panel per output, 12-bit).
  • Lowering the colour depth is the easiest way to win back refresh on long chains. Unlike the PocketScroller v3, a lower brightness setting lowers the refresh rate a little on the OctoPlus.

docs.title: FPP setup
docs.text:
When FPP detects the OctoPlus it sets up an LED Panels output (Input/Output Setup → Channel Outputs → LED Panels) with the OctoPlus wiring, starting with one 32×16 1/8-scan panel on Output 1. Change it to match your panels:

  1. Set the panel size and scan (e.g. 32×16 1/8, 64×32 1/16).
  2. Set the layout: how many panels wide and high.
  3. In the grid, assign each panel to an output and a position in the chain, and set its orientation.
  4. Set colour depth and brightness, then save. FPP restarts the output.

See LED panel matrices in the FPP manual for every field.

docs.text:

docs.title: Pi-OLED
docs.text:
An add-on for a Raspberry Pi running FPP: an OLED status display, four menu buttons, a real-time clock and a temperature sensor. It has no outputs of its own. It comes in two versions:

  • Pi-OLED 2.0 ("basic"): a narrow board held by the Pi's header.
  • PiOLED 3.0 With Audio: a full-size Pi hat that adds a high-quality audio output.

Use it on a Pi that drives its lights over the network or USB, or plays the show as a player or master: it gives the Pi the same display, menus and buttons as the Kulp controllers.

Not with an output hat

The Pi-OLED uses GPIO pins that the Kulp Pi controllers also use. Fit it to a Pi without another hat.

PiOLED 3.0 With Audio.

docs.text:
Sixteen HUB75 outputs for large LED panel matrices from a PocketBeagle 2. It's the bigger sibling of the PocketScroller v3, with the same power input, controls and expansion header, and twice the outputs.

PocketScroller-16 with a PocketBeagle 2 fitted.

This page covers board revision v3.0.0 (printed on the board as PocketScroller-16 v3.0.0). FPP calls it PocketScroller-16.

docs.text:
5 V only

Like the PocketScroller v3, the PocketScroller-16 has no voltage regulator. Connect a regulated 5 V supply to the terminal marked 5V / GND (top-right corner). A 12 V or 24 V supply makes the protection clamp conduct and trip the resettable fuse, and can damage the board.

  • The terminal powers the PocketBeagle 2, the panel drivers, Ethernet and the USB ports, not the panels. The board draws very little, but use a 5 V supply rated 5 A or more: it handles ripple and spikes better.
  • Power every panel from your 5 V panel supply. You can feed the PocketScroller-16 from the same supply.
  • There are no power LEDs. When the board is running, the OLED shows status.
  • FPP shows the input voltage as VIN.

docs.title: Panel outputs
docs.text:
The outputs are in two rows of eight: Output 1–8 across the upper row and Output 9–16 across the lower row, left to right.

Each is marked Output n below its connector, and each is a standard HUB75 connector. The pinout is the same as on the PocketScroller v3.

  • Use the ribbon cables that come with your panels. The red stripe goes to pin 1 (marked on the header's shroud).
  • Spread the panels evenly across the outputs. The refresh rate depends on the longest chain (see Capacity & refresh rate).

docs.text:
How many panels you can run depends on how long each chain is and on the colour depth. The table gives the full-frame refresh rate in Hz for 64×32 panels at FPP's default brightness (10). Bold values are 60 Hz or more. Italic values are under 60 Hz, where flicker starts to show on camera and to some viewers.

Panels per output Total panels 12-bit 10-bit 8-bit PWM panels (fps) 1 16 174 185 199 306 2 32 138 152 171 153 3 48 102 115 130 102 4 64 83 94 108 76 5 80 69 78 91 61 6 96 60 68 80 51 8 128 50 58 70 38 10 160 43 51 62 31 12 192 37 44 54 26 16 256 29 35 43 19

  • Refresh depends only on the longest chain. Every output is clocked whether or not a panel is attached, so using fewer outputs doesn't make it faster. Spread the panels evenly across all 16 outputs.
  • 1/8-scan outdoor panels refresh within a few percent of these 1/16-scan figures. Panels with shift-register row drivers ("ABC-shift" addressing, found on some outdoor 1/8 panels) are 7–16 % slower.
  • Lowering colour depth is the easiest way to win back refresh on long chains. Lowering the brightness setting raises refresh slightly (about 9 % at brightness 8).
  • The brightest bit plane is split into up to four pulses per frame, so the flicker a viewer actually sees runs 2–4× faster than the full-frame figure.

docs.text: Panels with PWM driver chips (FM6363C, FM6353, FM6373) run their own 16-bit greyscale, so they don't flicker as chains get longer. Chain length limits only how many new frames per second reach the panels: the last column of the table. Bold values there meet a 40 fps sequence, which works out to up to 7 panels per output (112 panels). Select the panel's driver chip under Panel Type in FPP's LED Panels settings.

docs.title: PocketScroller v2
docs.text:
Six HUB75 outputs for LED panel matrices, on a small board that works with either PocketBeagle.

PocketScroller v2 (v2.2) shown with an original PocketBeagle (PocketBeagle 1) fitted.

This page covers the PocketScroller v2, printed on the board as PocketScroller+ v2.x (the current revision is v2.3). Like the K4-PB and K40D-PB, it works with both the PocketBeagle 2 and the original PocketBeagle 1.

How the PocketScroller v2 differs from the other boards

  • No Ethernet on the board. Plug a USB Ethernet adapter or an FPP-supported USB Wi-Fi adapter into its USB-A port. You need one of them to set it up.
  • The USB-A port covers the PocketBeagle 2's SD card slot. To change the SD card you have to unplug the PocketBeagle 2. Either use a PocketBeagle 2 Industrial, which runs FPP from its built-in eMMC (recommended), or fit the PB2 microSD extender, which clears the USB port.
  • The OLED shares pins with output 6. If you use all six outputs, the OLED shows information while the board boots and then turns off once FPP starts. Leave output 6 free if you can.
  • No real-time clock. The board gets the time from the network (NTP).
  • 5 V only, like the other PocketScrollers.

PocketBeagle 1: never connect its USB port to a computer

With an original PocketBeagle 1 fitted, don't power or set up the PocketScroller v2 through the PocketBeagle's own USB port (USB tethering). It can permanently damage the board. With a PocketBeagle 2, USB tethering is safe.

docs.title: Power
docs.text:
5 V only

The PocketScroller v2 has no voltage regulator. Connect a regulated 5 V supply to the terminal at the top right, marked 5V (upper screw) and GND (lower screw). A 12 V or 24 V supply will damage the board and the PocketBeagle.

  • The terminal powers the PocketBeagle, the output buffer and the USB port. The board itself draws very little.
  • The panels are not powered through the PocketScroller. Run each panel's power from your 5 V panel supply. You can feed the PocketScroller from the same supply.
  • There are no power LEDs. When the board is running, the OLED shows status (as long as output 6 is free).

docs.title: Panel outputs
docs.text:
The six HUB75 outputs are along the bottom edge, Output 1 on the left to Output 6 on the right. They aren't numbered on the board. Connect each chain of panels with a 16-pin ribbon cable to the panel's input connector.

Output 6 and the OLED

The OLED's I²C lines share pins with output 6. While output 6 is unused, FPP keeps the OLED running. When you configure panels on output 6, FPP takes the pins for the panels and the OLED goes dark after boot. If you need fewer than six outputs, use outputs 1–5.

Set the panels up in FPP under Input/Output Setup → Channel Outputs → LED Panels. See LED panel matrices in the FPP manual.

docs.text:
The two buttons at the top left are marked Down (left) and Enter (right). The left button is also Test: on the status page it starts and cycles the test patterns; in menus it moves down. See Controls & display.

The OLED plugs into the 4-pin socket marked GND 3.3V SCL SDA.

docs.text:
How many panels you can run depends on how long each chain is and on the colour depth. The tables give the full-frame refresh rate in Hz for 64×32, 1/16-scan panels at FPP's default brightness (10), with all six outputs in use. Bold values are 60 Hz or more. Italic values are under 60 Hz, where flicker starts to show on camera and to some viewers.

Rule of thumb at 60 Hz: up to 2 panels per output at 12-bit colour (12 panels), or 4 per output at 8-bit (24 panels).

Rule of thumb at 60 Hz: up to 3 panels per output at 12-bit colour (18 panels), or 5 per output at 8-bit (30 panels).

  • These are measured, worst-case figures, with random pixel data on every panel. Flat colours and large solid areas refresh faster, by up to about 40 %.
  • The PocketBeagle 1 is faster on longer chains. Past 2 panels per output the PocketScroller v2 runs about 25 % slower on a PocketBeagle 2. If you need the most panels at a high refresh rate, the PocketScroller v3 or PocketScroller-16 is a better fit on a PocketBeagle 2.

  • Lowering colour depth is the easiest way to win back refresh. Unlike the v3 and -16, lowering the brightness setting makes the PocketScroller v2 slightly slower, because it adds off-time.

docs.text:
When FPP detects the PocketScroller v2 it offers the PocketScroller wiring for LED panels. Add an LED Panels output and your panel layout under Input/Output Setup → Channel Outputs → LED Panels.

  • Rule of thumb at 60 Hz: up to 10 panels per output at 12-bit colour (80 panels), or 16 per output at 8-bit (128 panels).
  • Refresh depends only on the longest chain. Every output is clocked whether or not a panel is attached, so using fewer outputs doesn't make it faster. Spread the panels evenly across all 8 outputs.
  • 1/8-scan outdoor panels refresh within a few percent of these 1/16-scan figures. Panels with shift-register row drivers ("ABC-shift" addressing, found on some outdoor 1/8 panels) are 7–16 % slower.
  • Lowering colour depth is the easiest way to win back refresh on long chains. Lowering the brightness setting raises refresh slightly (about 9 % at brightness 8).
  • The brightest bit plane is split into up to four pulses per frame, so the flicker a viewer actually sees runs 2–4× faster than the full-frame figure.

Estimated figures

These numbers come from FPP's refresh estimator for the 8-output firmware. On the PocketScroller-16 the same estimator matched hardware measurements to within 0.5 %, but the 8-output timing hasn't been measured on a board yet.

docs.title: PWM panels
docs.text: Panels with PWM driver chips (FM6363C, FM6353, FM6373) run their own 16-bit greyscale, so they don't flicker as chains get longer. Chain length limits only how many new frames per second reach the panels: the last column of the table. Bold values there meet a 40 fps sequence, which works out to up to 12 panels per output (96 panels). Select the panel's driver chip under Panel Type in FPP's LED Panels settings.

docs.title: FPP setup
docs.text:
When FPP detects the PocketScroller it sets up an LED Panels output (Input/Output Setup → Channel Outputs → LED Panels) with the PocketScroller v3 wiring. The starting layout is a 2×2 block of 64×32 panels at low brightness. Change it to match your panels:

  1. Set the panel size and scan (e.g. 64×32 1/16, 64×64 1/32).
  2. Set the layout: how many panels wide and high.
  3. In the grid, assign each panel to an output and a position in the chain, and set its orientation.
  4. Set colour depth and brightness, then save. FPP restarts the output.

See LED panel matrices in the FPP manual for every field.

docs.title: Dimensions & mounting
docs.text:
• 121.95 × 100.70 mm (4.80 × 3.96 in), 6 plated mounting holes, 3.0 mm, for M2.5 (or #4) screws and standoffs.

docs.title: Quick start
docs.text: Work through this list in order. Each step finishes with a check, so if something goes wrong you know which step it was.

docs.title: What you need
docs.text:
• [ ] The controller, with a PocketBeagle 2, BeagleBone Black or Raspberry Pi fitted (see PocketBeagle 2, BeagleBone Black or Raspberry Pi)
  • [ ] A microSD card with FPP, unless you have a PB2 Industrial with FPP on eMMC
  • [ ] A 5–24 V DC LED power supply matched to your pixels (5 V only for the PocketScrollers, K40D-PB, K64D-B, K128D-B and OctoPlus; 18 V at most for the K8-PB, K4-PB, K8-B, K8-B-Scroller and K8-Pi)
  • [ ] An Ethernet cable to your router or show switch. The K8-PB, K4-PB, K40D-PB and PocketScroller v2 have no Ethernet jack, so they also need a USB Ethernet adapter (or a USB Wi-Fi adapter).
  • [ ] Pixels with a pigtail wired to a 3-pin plug (or LED panels for the PocketScrollers and OctoPlus)
  • [ ] A small flat screwdriver

docs.title: 1. Bench test with one string
docs.text:
On the K40D-PB, K64D-B and K128D-B, which have no pixel ports, wire the string to a differential receiver on the 1-4 jack instead, and power the board from a 5 V supply.

  1. [ ] Read Safety.
  2. [ ] Insert the SD card into the PocketBeagle 2, BeagleBone or Pi, unless you are using eMMC.
  3. [ ] Wire one pixel string to P1: ground in G, data in D, +V in V. Check the pixel voltage matches your supply.
  4. [ ] Check the supply before connecting it: set its 115V/230V input switch (if it has one) to match your mains, then plug it in and measure the DC output with a multimeter. Unplug it again before wiring. See Check the supply.
  5. [ ] Wire the supply to the terminal that powers the controller. That's the terminal for ports 1–4 on the K16 and K32, and the right-hand terminal on the K8 boards. On the K8 boards, P1 is fed from the left terminal, so for this test wire both K8 terminals, or use P5 instead. The K8-PB, K4-PB, K8-B, K8-B-Scroller, K8-Pi and K2-Pi0 have a single terminal for everything; on the K2-Pi-Servo, use the top (pixel) terminal. See Power.
  6. [ ] Plug in the Ethernet cable (on the K8-PB, K4-PB, K40D-PB or PocketScroller v2, through the USB Ethernet adapter).
  7. [ ] Plug the supply into the mains.

Check: the power LEDs light (on the K8-B and K8-B-Scroller, the green LED above each fuse), and within a minute or two the OLED shows the FPP logo and then the status page with an IP address. The first boot of a new SD card can take a few minutes longer.

docs.title: 2. Connect to FPP
docs.text:
1. [ ] On a computer on the same network, open a browser to the IP address on the OLED, or to http://fpp.local.
  2. [ ] Work through FPP's first-time setup: hostname, time zone and so on. See Initial configuration.

Check: the FPP status page shows your board under the cape name, and the header shows the input voltage(s).

docs.title: 3. Light the string
docs.text:
1. [ ] Press Test on the controller.

Check: the string on P1 cycles red, green and blue. Press Test until the OLED shows Off.

If nothing lights, see Troubleshooting → No pixels light.

docs.title: 4. Configure your show
docs.text:
1. [ ] In xLights, add the controller as an FPP controller with your board as the model, map your props to its ports, and use Upload Outputs to send the port configuration. See Configuring outputs.
  2. [ ] Upload sequences and audio with FPP Connect, then build a playlist and a schedule in FPP.

docs.title: 5. Install
docs.text:
1. [ ] Main Menu → Shutdown (or shut down from FPP), then remove power.
  2. [ ] Mount the controller in its enclosure. Wire the remaining banks and ports, then the differential receivers.
  3. [ ] Power up and run the Test patterns again to check every port.

Back up

Once it's working, save a backup from FPP (Status/Control → FPP Backup). See Backup.

docs.title: Safety
docs.text:
These controllers run on low-voltage DC (5–24 V) but can switch a lot of current. A K32 with every port loaded can deliver well over 100 A across its banks. At that level, the hazards are fire from loose or undersized wiring, and the mains (AC) side of your power supplies.

Mains voltage

  • Never connect household AC (120/230 V) to any terminal on the controller. The controller only accepts DC from a power supply.
  • Have the AC side of your power supplies wired by someone qualified. Use grounded (3-prong) cords and close the terminal covers on the supply.
  • If a supply has a 115V/230V input switch, set it to match your mains before you plug it in. The wrong setting can destroy the supply.
  • Unplug the AC before you touch the supply's output terminals or the controller's power terminals.

Fire prevention

  • Never fit a larger fuse than the one supplied, and never bridge a fuse holder. The fuse protects the pixel wiring; a bigger fuse lets that wiring overheat.
  • Use wire rated for the current it carries (see Power → Wire size). Tighten every screw terminal firmly. A loose terminal heats up under load.
  • Tin or ferrule stranded wire ends. Stray strands can short to the next terminal.
  • Mount the controller in an enclosure, away from flammable material. Leave room for airflow, especially around the power terminals and the eFuse/fuse area.

Polarity and voltage

  • Check V+ and G/V− on every terminal before you power up. On the K8, K16 and K32 boards the power inputs have reverse-polarity protection, so reversed power won't damage the controller; that bank simply stays off. The K8-PB and K4-PB have no such protection, and a reversed supply can damage them. Pixels have no such protection either. Wiring a pixel string backwards, or running 5 V pixels from a 12 V bank, will destroy the pixels.
  • Every pixel port on a bank gets the voltage of that bank's power supply. Check that the supply voltage matches the pixels on every port in the bank.
  • The K40D-PB and the PocketScrollers accept 5 V only. Do not connect 12 V or 24 V to them.

Outdoors

The controller is not waterproof. Outdoors, mount it in a weather-resistant enclosure with drip loops on every cable, and keep the power supplies in an enclosure too. Condensation and insects cause more failures than rain does.

Making connections

Turn the power off before you plug or unplug pixel connectors, receivers or power terminals. Network, USB, audio and DMX cables can be connected with the power on.

Storage

If you store the controller for a long time, take out the clock (RTC) coin cell. That keeps it from draining and leaking.
